Exposition devoted to Gramophone and radio sets

A cart, cart — an ancient type of transport designed for transporting goods and people, used in conjunction with a harness. A cart consists of such main parts as a shaft (ara–vashoti), a wheel (tegarchik) and an axle. A shaft consists of two 4.5 m long horse–drawn carriages (atliq), 8 pogona, two soloq and aygiz. Horse–drawn carriages are made of poplar. The shafts (70–80 cm in length) have one hole at each end to fasten the horse\'s neck.\n A wheel (tegarchik) consists of such parts as a gupchak, togyn, kegay, bellik, aravatemir, aravamikh and a pillow. Aravatemir and aravamikh are made of iron, and other parts are made of a type of resin (bujun) of kayragoch. The shaft is a piece of polished wood 40 cm thick and 2.5 m long, with both ends inserted into a round hole and a cart shaft mounted on it. A slat is placed under it to prevent the shaft from slipping while moving. Carts have two, three, and four wheels. Depending on the type of vehicle they are attached to, they are of different types, such as horse-drawn carts, camel carts, ox carts, and donkey carts.

Postal service is a system of institutions that receive and send letters, periodicals, parcels, money, etc. using means of transport. The emergence of postal service is directly related to the emergence of writing. In the Greek, Iranian, Egyptian, Chinese and Roman empires, postal service was of particular importance in state administration, and state postal service was well established: sent letters were transported on horseback and on foot on the principle of relays. With the development of crafts and trade, city post offices appeared that served artisans and merchants. At the same time, they also served other segments of the population.\nIn the 16th and 17th centuries, centralized royal post offices appeared in France, Sweden, England, and other countries. With the growth of postal communication and the development of interstate economic relations, postal communication also developed. The introduction of postal stamps into circulation marked a new era in the history of postal communication. In 1869, the postcard was introduced in Austria. In 1874, the 1st International Postal Congress was held with the participation of 22 countries, and an agreement was signed on the establishment of the Universal Postal Union (since 1878, the Universal Postal Union). In 1978, the Universal Postal Union Convention was adopted to coordinate correspondence and the exchange of written information around the world. The creation of steamships and locomotives at the beginning of the 19th century, and airplanes at the beginning of the 20th century, dramatically increased the speed of delivering mail. Postal services began to be used not only by the state, but also by ordinary citizens. The invention of the telegraph (1832), the telephone (1876), and the radio (1895) did not change the important place that postal communication held in the life of society. Even in the 20th century, it remained the most convenient and popular means of communication.

A television tower is a support on which the antennas of a television transmitting station are mounted. Sometimes the word "tower" is used, but it is slang and is no longer used in this sense.The zone of reliable reception of television and broadcasting signals depends on the height of the transmitting antennas on the television tower, so they are built as high as possible and placed at the highest points on the ground. The zone also depends on the power of the transmitters, so large television centers consume a large amount of electricity. The large capacity of the transmission cables (feeders), as well as their height and specific design, increase the likelihood of fires, which are very difficult to extinguish.

Money is a special commodity that acts as a general equivalent for all other commodities. Money plays a major role in the exchange of common commodities. In ancient times, various commodities served as money, such as cattle, hides, axes, etc. Later, precious metals served as money, because they did not lose their value and were very useful as a substitute for money. Money is not just a commodity, it has social value, that is, it serves as a means of purchasing all goods.

Gramophone (Greek gramma - letter, writing and phone - sound) - a device for reproducing sound recorded on a gramophone. In the groove of a rotating gramophone, the vibrations of the G. needle are transmitted to a membrane that is amplified by a speaker. A compact version of the G. is the phonograph. Since the 1950s, the electrophonium has been used instead of the G.

A radio receiver (abbreviated as receiver, colloquially as radio) is a device connected to an antenna and used for radio reception, that is, for the separation of signals from radio waves.A radio receiver is a radio receiver equipped with an antenna, as well as means for processing the received information and reproducing it in the desired form (visual, audio, printed text, etc.). In most cases, the antenna and the reproducing means are systematically part of the radio receiver. A radio receiver uses an antenna to spatially and polarize radio waves and convert them into electrical radio signals (voltage, current), change the frequency, separate the useful radio signal from the set of other (interfering) signals and noise that act at the output of the receiving antenna and do not coincide in frequency with the useful signal, amplify it, and convert the useful radio signal into a form that allows the use of the information contained in it. Officially, radio receivers are included in radio stations, although such a classification is rarely found in practice.

Radio (Latin radius - "light") is a technology for wireless transmission of signals using electromagnetic waves./nRadio (Latin radio - I radiate, I spread light) - 1) a method of wireless transmission and reception of information over long distances using radio waves (electromagnetic waves). Invented in 1895 by A. S. Popov; 2) a branch of science and technology related to the study of physical phenomena based on the method of wireless transmission, the use of this method in radio communications, radio broadcasting, television, radio telemechanics, radar, automation of production processes, remote control (telecontrol), medicine and other purposes

The earliest practical recording technologies were entirely mechanical devices. These recorders typically used a large conical horn to collect and focus the physical air pressure of the sound waves produced by the human voice or musical instruments. A sensitive membrane or diaphragm, located at the apex of the cone, was connected to an articulated scriber or stylus, and as the changing air pressure moved the diaphragm back and forth, the stylus scratched or incised an analog of the sound waves onto a moving recording medium, such as a roll of coated paper, or a cylinder or disc coated with a soft material such as wax or a soft metal.

A phonograph, later called a gramophone (as a trademark since 1887, as a generic name in the UK since 1910), and since the 1940s a record player, or more recently a turntable, is a device for the mechanical and analogue reproduction of sound.[a] The sound vibration waveforms are recorded as corresponding physical deviations of a helical or spiral groove engraved, etched, incised, or impressed into the surface of a rotating cylinder or disc, called a record. To recreate the sound, the surface is similarly rotated while a playback stylus traces the groove and is therefore vibrated by it, faintly reproducing the recorded sound. In early acoustic phonographs, the stylus vibrated a diaphragm that produced sound waves coupled to the open air through a flaring horn, or directly to the listener\'s ears through stethoscope-type earphones.

Gramophone (from the French company name "Pathe" and … phonograph) is a type of gramophone, a device used to reproduce sound recorded on a gramophone record. The first P. had a large speaker, later the speaker was placed in a box. The disc was rotated by a spring that was tensioned by turning it with a handle. P. was used until the 1950s. It is still kept in some homes and museums.

An automatic switch (also circuit breaker) is a contact switching device (mechanical or electronic) capable of turning on currents, conducting them, and turning them off under normal conditions in a circuit, as well as turning on, conducting them for a specified (set) time, and automatically turning off currents under specified abnormal conditions in a circuit, such as short-circuit currents.

Morse code is an electromagnetic telegraph device that transmits and receives signals using Morse code. It was invented and used in practice by S. Morse in 1844. Its structure is simple, it works well, but the speed of transmitting and receiving signals is low. The Morse code device mainly consists of a transmitter (switch) and a receiver (see figure k,.). To transmit signals, the switch K and the battery B are connected in accordance with the Morse code. Current flows through the electromagnet E, attracting the core armature Ya. As a result, the painted recording pad (PK) touches the tape, leaving a long and short mark on it. The tape is continuously driven by a clock mechanism. The speed of the tape can be 160–180 cm/min. Using the Morse code device, 950–1100 words per hour can be transmitted over a 5 mm steel wire up to 500 km.
History of the 6N-1 tube radio receiver

6The Voronezh Electrosignal plant had been producing the 6NG-1 network tube radio since the fall of 1937. Since 1938, the receiver was put into serial production, and by the end of May it was called the 6N-1 (6-tube, Tabletop, 1st model). The basis for development was the RCA Victor 6T2 receiver. The first receivers were equipped with metal tubes from RCA, Ken-Rad, Tung-Sol and others.

KVN-49 (an abbreviation of the developers\' surnames Kenigson, Varshavsky, Nikolaevsky, 1949) is a black-and-white television set produced in the USSR in various modifications from 1949 to 1962. The first mass-produced television set in the USSR and one of the first in the world designed for the 625/50 resolution standard adopted in the Soviet Union in 1945. In 1944, the USSR began developing a 625-line black-and-white television standard.
History of the cathode ray tube

A cathode ray tube is an electron-ray device that converts electrical signals into visible images and optical images into electrical signals. Electron-ray tubes that convert electrical signals into visible images include oscillographic indicator cathode-ray tubes, kinescopes, etc., while electron-ray tubes that convert optical images into electrical signals include, for example, transmitting television tubes. There are also cathode-ray tubes in which both the input and output signals are in the form of electrical signals. Such tubes represent some kind of transformation, for example, mathematical processing, a change in the frequency spectrum, and other physical processes.

Luna 24 was a robotic probe of the Soviet Union\'s Luna programme. The 24th mission of the Luna series of spacecraft, the mission of the Luna 24 probe was the third Soviet mission to return lunar soil samples from the Moon (the first two sample return missions were Luna 16 and Luna 20). The probe landed in Mare Crisium (Sea of Crises). The mission returned 170.1 g (6.00 oz) of lunar samples to the Earth on 22 August 1976.
History of the typewriter telegraph machine

Telegraph apparatus - a device designed to transmit and receive electrical signals in telegraph communication. The first electromagnetic telegraph apparatus was invented by the Russian scientist P. L. Schilling (1832) and was used in practice. In the first electromagnetic apparatus, messages were transmitted and recorded in the form of broken lines (recording telegraph apparatus) or dotted lines (recording telegraph apparatus) or dots and dashes (see Morse apparatus). Until the middle of the 20th century, an electromechanical telegraph apparatus was used, starting from the 70s, an electromechanical telegraph apparatus was used, later a fully electronic telegraph apparatus and a phototelegraph apparatus (facsimile apparatus) appeared.

A telephone set is an electroacoustic device designed for subscribers to talk; the last subscriber device in telephone networks. The first transmission receiving device used in practice was invented in 1876 by the Scottish inventor A.G. Bell. Later, inventors and scientists from different countries improved it. The telephone set consists of a talking part (a telephone and a microphone, which are combined into a common housing, i.e. a tube), a subscriber calling part (a dialer with a disc or button, i.e. a signal bell) and a switching device (connecting the calling part of the device to the talking part). All telephone sets operate in a mechanoautomatic mode (i.e. dialing is mechanical, and connecting subscribers is carried out automatically). There are also automatic telephone sets with an autodialer that "itself" answers subscribers and records their telephone numbers in magnetic memory.
